Don't stretch your calves if you have plantar fasciitis. Do this instead.

I'm going to say something that no one who's had heel pain for years wants to hear. And I don't give a sh*t if it upsets you.

The cortisone shot won't fix this. The night splint won't. The frozen water bottle won't. Those $180 cloud sneakers all over your feed? Those won't either. The next podiatrist appointment won't.

And that "6 to 18 months, it usually clears up on its own"? That's just going to sit there and watch your foot get worse.

Not 1 thing on that list is touching what's really causing your pain. I know. I watched my mother deal with the same thing.

10 years of Ice. Inserts. 2 rounds of shots. Then a surgery that was meant to fix it all, where they cut the band in her foot to release it. It never held right after that. A cane, then a walker. No body could ever fix it.

Then, 1 year ago, I sat on the edge of my bed at 5:40 AM and couldn't put my right foot flat on the floor.

It's happening to me. And if you sat on the edge of your bed this morning working yourself up to that first step, it's happening to you.

So read every word. It's long. But the answer is in here. And it is NOT another treatment.

I'm Denise. I'm 59, from Mansfield, Ohio. I was a nursing home aide for 26 years. On my feet all day. Lifting, turning, hauling. The lot.

For me it started small. A twinge getting up off the couch after the 10 o'clock news. A little bruised feeling under my right heel. Nothing a hot soak wouldn't sort.

2 months later it wasn't small. It was a nail through my heel every morning. Standing up made me gasp out loud.

Some days it screamed. Some days it went almost quiet. I couldn't work it out. I thought the tissue in my foot was shredding a little more every week. It wasn't. (Hold that thought. It matters later.)

I did what you're meant to do. I called the office. Waited 3 weeks. Got 10 minutes with a doctor who never looked up from the screen. "Plantar fasciitis. Common at your age. Ice it. Stretch it. Lose a bit of weight." Out the door.

The pharmacy sold me gel inserts. For 2 weeks it was almost a miracle. Then it stopped. And when the pain came back, it came back meaner. Deeper. The kind no cushion could reach, because it wasn't coming from the surface.

By then I'd joined 1 of those Facebook foot pain groups. Thousands of us. All hobbling to the bathroom at dawn. All with a tip. A night splint. A frozen water bottle. A massage gun. Compression sleeves. KT tape. Turmeric. A $40 pair of heel cups off Amazon. CBD balm. 2 more pairs of drugstore orthotics. $200 max-cushion sneakers that everyone swore were like walking on clouds and that had me limping by Thursday.

I spent over $400 on sh*t in 4 months. And I still couldn't pull my own socks on without holding my breath.

Then it hit me like cold water. I was doing exactly what my mother did. The same ice. The same inserts. The same "give it time." Walking her road, step by step. Towards the same chair.

They'd always told us flat feet "run in families." Nobody told me the truth. We were both treating the wrong damn thing.

By August I was a ghost. I couldn't stand long enough to make a real dinner. I couldn't walk the dog past the second mailbox before the pain had me leaning on somebody's fence like an old woman. I stopped going to my grandson's Little League. I sat down to fold laundry. And I'd be up at 5:00 AM on the edge of the bed, working up to that first step. Crying. Swearing into my sleeve so I didn't wake my husband.

The woman who used to close down every wedding reception in Richland County was googling "mobility scooter" at 2:00 in the morning. I thought I was just getting old. I wasn't. That was wrong too.

Back to the doctor. He sent me to a podiatrist. The wait was 6 weeks. And a quick mention of custom orthotics. $600, not covered.

I paid for 1 physical therapy visit I couldn't afford. $55 for 3 stretches off a printout. "Keep at them. Give it more time." More time. While that foot ate me alive every morning.

So I did the stretches. Morning and night. And here's the thing nobody warned me about: they made it worse. I know why now. That band under your foot isn't tight like a muscle. It's torn. Overnight your body knits those tiny tears back together. Then you get up and haul on it first thing and rip every 1 of them open again. Every stretch was me tearing it back open.

That's why I say don't stretch your calves. Nobody ever told me the stretching was part of the problem.

The discharge paper even admitted it: "Most cases resolve within 6 to 18 months." That's not a treatment plan. That's a shrug on letterhead.

So I stopped hunting for another treatment. And I started hunting for the cause.

Once I saw it, I couldn't un-see it. Look at the road they marched me down. My mother before me.

A twinge. Ice. An insert. It fades. Better sneakers. A shot. Another shot. $600 orthotics. Surgery. A chair.

Every step just managed the pain. Not 1 step ever asked WHY it was there. We were all mopping up the puddle and wondering why the bastard kept coming back.

I'd already ruled out the easy stuff. New shoes, twice. 15 pounds gone. None of it touched the pain. Because none of it reached where the problem really lived. Not my skin. Not even really my foot. Somewhere underneath it.

I spent 2 weeks reading. Not the sponsored stuff. The real threads. Reddit at 4:00 AM. Forums full of people who'd suffered 20 years. Physical therapists on YouTube who'd gone "off-script" from the usual advice.

Then I found 1 comment. Buried under a post. From a retired mail carrier in Oregon.

"Mine burned for 6 years. I tried it all. What finally settled it wasn't a treatment. Take the insole out of the shoe you wore yesterday. Put it next to a brand new one. Look at them both from the side."

From the side. Not how it feels under your thumb. From the side. I read it 10 times.

I did it that night. Mine was flatter. Then I talked myself out of it, because it still felt soft when I pressed it.

So I ordered the first thing I could find. $17 gel insoles off Amazon. Thousands of 5-star reviews.

Week 1: nothing.

Week 2: nothing.

Week 3: still turning around at that second mailbox, I nearly wrote it all off as more snake oil.

What saved me was a chat over the back fence. My neighbor Marlene is 71. She was a certified orthotist for 35 years. Half of them in a foot and ankle clinic in Columbus. She saw me come down my porch steps sideways, 1 at a time, and came over. I showed her the insoles. She laughed, kindly.

"Oh, honey. These are worse than useless. No wonder they've done nothing. Do you want to know why?"

And standing there in her slippers, she told me the thing no 10-minute appointment ever had.

"Your arch isn't a stack of bones that holds itself up. It's a bridge, and there's a band strung underneath holding the 2 ends together. Every step, your whole weight comes down and that arch drops. It's meant to drop, that's how a foot takes a step. The only thing that has ever mattered is what's underneath it when it does.

Out on dirt, on grass, on uneven ground, the ground comes up and catches it. On a concrete floor in a flat shoe, nothing does. That band catches all of it. 10,000 times a day. And after 50 it's worse, because the fat pad under your heel has thinned and that band's gone stiff. Less padding, less give. Same concrete you stood on at 30.

That's the whole job of an insole. Be there at the bottom of the step. And almost every insole you can buy fails at it. There are only 2 ways it happens.

The soft ones pancake. They feel supportive because they push back against your thumb. Your thumb isn't 180 pounds. Under your real weight it bottoms out — flat, at the exact instant your arch is dropping, the 1 instant it had a job to do. And it doesn't happen all at once. A new one holds a little. Every day crushes it down further and it comes back less, until it doesn't come back at all.

That's why they work for a few weeks and then quit on you. You weren't imagining that.

The other kind doesn't collapse. It just hurts. Rock-hard and bulky, the sort you rip out by lunchtime and leave in a drawer. That's what your $600 is going to buy you.

So you've got one that gives out and one you won't wear. Either way, by the end of the day that arch is dropping onto nothing.

Cushion is what a thing feels like when you're not standing on it. Holding is what it does when you are. Once it's flat it isn't doing anything. It's a floor with a logo on it."

First time in 1 year, something made sense.

Then she told me why everything I'd bought had failed. And it wasn't bad luck.

"The shots? They quiet the pain for a few weeks, then fade. They never hold anything up. It's like watering the leaves of a plant when the roots are dry. The night splint? It holds your foot while you sleep. You're not doing the damage in your sleep. You're doing it in the 14 hours you're upright. The ice, the sleeve, the cloud sneakers? The softer the shoe, the further that arch falls before anything stops it. You went out and bought the thing that lets it drop the farthest. Not 1 of them holds an arch. You were standing on hope."

Not all insoles are the same, she said. It's what's under the arch. Whether it's still holding when your weight comes down. And whether you can stand to keep it in all day.

"This," she said, "is what I'd have sent my patients home in. If we'd ever been allowed to sell anything. It's called Xstance."

She set 1 on her step, put her foot on it, and put her whole weight down. It didn't move.

"They call it the Triple Support System, and it's the only one I know of that answers both failure modes at once.

A precision arch stabilizer, still holding at the bottom of the step, when it counts.

An impact cushioning heel pad set inside a deep, walled heel cup, right underneath the spot taking the beating. What padding you've got left under that heel bone squirts out sideways when you land. The cup keeps it under the bone instead of around it.

And a soft silicone comfort layer from heel to toe. That's the part your foot touches. Soft where it touches you, firm where your weight lands. That's why it isn't the rigid kind you rip out at lunch.

Rigid enough that it won't collapse under you. Soft enough that you'll actually leave it in. Most insoles only ever manage one of those.

The real test isn't how it feels when you put your shoes on at 6 AM. It's whether it's still holding at hour eleven.”

That was the whole difference. The 1 thing I'd been missing for 1 year.

Then she told me the part I nearly got wrong.

"If you've only got 1 pair, you're only fixing it some of the time. You switch between your sneakers and your work shoes and your slippers, and your feet are shifting between something holding and nothing holding. Every day you go back to a flat shoe, you undo the ground you just made. Put a pair in every set of shoes you wear."

You put them in and you wear them every day, in every pair. That's the whole thing. Nothing to swallow. Nothing to fog your head. Nothing to clash with your other tablets. And they come with a 90-day money-back promise. So the only thing I could lose was a few more weeks of the same.

And here's what made me cry with anger.

There's a billing code for the shot. There's a code for the imaging. There's a code for the $600 custom pair and there's a code for the surgery that put my mother in that chair. There is no code on God's earth for "your insoles went flat in March and you've been standing on nothing since." The system is built to walk you towards the codes. Not to look inside your shoe. Nobody gets paid to tell a woman in Mansfield what's under her arch.

The system's hands are tied. Yours are not.

So I started. Every day. Every pair. No excuses.

Week 1: I got from the bed to the coffee pot without the counter.

Week 2: I stood a whole shift. I cried in the car afterwards. The good kind.

Week 3: I walked the dog to the second mailbox. Then past it. All the way to the reservoir and back. And I never once reached for a fence.

By week 5 I was kneeling in the garden with my hands in the soil. And when my grandson hollered "Grandma, watch this!" at his Little League game, I was at that fence, on my feet, cheering like I used to.

The first step in the morning. The socks I couldn't reach. The dancing I'd given up. 1 by 1, they came back.

Marlene checked my insoles a few months in. The way she'd checked 1,000 feet. She set them on her step and put her weight down.

"Still holding," she said. "Not a millimeter. In 35 years I hardly ever saw a foot this angry settle this well without a knife. And you did it with an insole and a bit of patience."

That was 8 months ago. Not 1 bad morning since. My feet are quiet. I gave a pair to my sister, who'd started down the same road. Hers is settling too. This isn't a good week that wears off. It held. It's still holding.

I think about my mother every single day. That chair. That window. The garden she never got back to. And the last thing she said to me.

If you're reading this on the edge of your bed working up to that first step, do not walk her road. Do not wait out 6 to 18 months while it takes your job and your walks and your Saturdays. Do not hand your good years over the way she did.

"Just as I suspected… your foot pain is not Plantar Fasciitis. It's Baxter's Nerve Entrapment."

"Baxter's… what?"

I stared at Dr. Navarro like she'd just spoken another language.

She pulled up my imaging on her screen and pointed to a spot near the inside of my heel.

"There's a small nerve that runs along the bottom of your foot. It's called the inferior calcaneal nerve.

Most people have never heard of it.

When that nerve gets compressed or damaged, it causes pain in the exact same spot as Plantar Fasciitis.

Same location.
Same morning agony.
Same heel.

But it's a completely different problem. Your fascia looks fine. It's the nerve that's in trouble."

===========

I sat there with my mouth open.

"But three different doctors told me it was Plantar Fasciitis."

Dr. Navarro nodded like she'd heard this a hundred times.

"Up to 20% of chronic heel pain cases are actually nerve-related. Not fascia-related.

But most providers see heel pain and go straight to the PF diagnosis without ever testing the nerve.

That's why nothing has worked for you. You've been treating the wrong tissue."

===========

She explained that what was happening inside my foot was something she called a Three-System Nerve Collapse.

System 1: Nerve Signal Disruption

- The compressed nerve starts misfiring

- It sends pain signals even when you're sitting still

- Burning. Tingling. That weird electric feeling in your sole

- Standard PF treatments like orthotics and stretching don't touch nerve signals

- They're designed for connective tissue. Not nerve tissue

- So the nerve keeps misfiring no matter how many insoles you buy

System 2: Myelin Breakdown

- Every nerve fiber is wrapped in a protective coating called myelin

- Think of it like the rubber insulation around an electrical wire

- When that coating breaks down, the nerve becomes exposed

- Exposed nerves are hypersensitive to pressure, temperature, and movement

- That's why your heel screams when you step on a hard floor

- That's why the pain feels electric instead of just sore

- Once myelin starts degrading, it doesn't rebuild on its own without the right building blocks

System 3: Inflammatory Nerve Damage

- Your body's inflammatory response was supposed to be temporary

- But when a nerve is compressed for months, the inflammation becomes chronic

- Chronic inflammation releases enzymes that eat away at the nerve fiber itself

- Shots can calm the inflammation for a few weeks

- But they don't stop the enzymes from continuing to damage the nerve

- Repeated shots near a nerve can actually make things worse

- The inflammation keeps cycling. The nerve keeps degrading

===========

Then she asked me a question that stopped me cold.

"Does the pain feel like a sharp stab?
Or more like burning, tingling, or numbness?"

I didn't even have to think about it.

"Burning. Definitely burning.
Sometimes tingling.
Sometimes my heel just goes numb for no reason."

She nodded.

"That's the giveaway. 

Here's how to know the difference in 5 seconds:

If the pain is:

- On the BOTTOM of your heel

- A sharp, stabbing feeling

- Worst on those very first steps in the morning

- Eases up once you start moving around

- Comes back after long periods on your feet

That's likely Plantar Fasciitis.

But if the pain is:

- Burning, tingling, or numbness in your heel or sole

- An electric or radiating sensation, not a sharp stab

- Doesn't ease up with movement. Sometimes gets WORSE

- Flares up at night when you're off your feet

- Comes with random shooting pains you can't predict

That's nerve-origin heel pain.

And no amount of stretching or orthotics will fix it.

Because the problem was never your fascia.

It's your nerve."

===========

Everything suddenly made sense.

===========

Why the custom orthotics helped my arch but did nothing for the burning under my heel.

Why the shot gave me two decent weeks and then the pain roared back.

Why the night splint made the stiffness slightly better but the tingling worse.

Why the stretching exercises my first doctor gave me felt completely pointless.

Why I'd wake up at 3 AM with my heel on fire even though I hadn't been on my feet for hours.

I wasn't failing the treatments.

The treatments were failing me.

Because they were designed for a tissue problem.

And I had a nerve problem.

===========

"So what actually fixes this?"

I was almost afraid to hear the answer.

Dr. Navarro pulled out a notepad.

"We need to address the nerve damage at three levels," she said.

"First, we need to calm the nerve itself. Stop the misfiring. Reduce the hypersensitivity. Your body makes a molecule called PEA that does exactly this.

But when a nerve has been inflamed for months, your local PEA supply gets depleted. We need to replenish it directly at the nerve site."

"Second, we need to feed the myelin sheath. Give it the raw materials to rebuild. That means B-vitamins in their active forms. 

Methylcobalamin. Benfotiamine. Plus GLA from plant oils. These are the building blocks your nerve coating needs to repair."

"Third, we need to support cellular energy at the nerve level. Damaged nerves are energy-starved. CoQ10 powers the mitochondria inside nerve cells.

I'm going to say something that nobody with plantar fasciitis wants to hear. As long as you believe resting will fix it, it won't heal.

Not in six months. Not in a year. Not ever.

I know that because I believed it for two and a half years, and I did it better than most people ever do.

For almost my entire life, I was a runner.

Not casually either. Thirty to forty miles a week since my twenties. I'm 45 now.

The rest of my life looks like this. I sit at a desk for nine hours, I come home, and I run. That's been the shape of my days for close to twenty years.

I never thought about my feet because they never gave me a reason to.

Then one morning I stood up out of bed and my right heel felt like I'd stepped on broken glass.

That was the beginning of two and a half years.

I'm going to tell you everything I tried, in order.

Here's what the first six months looked like.

The pain showed up after runs. Then during runs. Then it stopped waiting for runs at all and just lived there.

And it went past stepping on broken glass.

It became a nail driven into my heel, or a Lego brick pressed into it, all day long.

I tried explaining it to people. Nobody ever really understood.

By month four I couldn't walk to the mailbox without limping the first twenty steps.

So I did what everyone tells you to do first.

I stopped running. Completely. Not reduced. Stopped.

Six weeks of nothing.

I never really got back to running after that. A mile here and there, always paid for the next morning.

And here's the first thing that confused me. The rest didn't help.

It got slightly better for about four days, then it plateaued, and by week five it was getting worse while I was doing absolutely nothing.

It made no sense to me, and it never stopped making no sense.

Then I started testing everything else, one at a time, because if you change five things at once you learn nothing.

I started with the shoes, because that's what everyone says.

Eight pairs. Every one of them followed the same pattern. The first two hours felt better and I'd think, this is the one. Then the afternoon came, and the pain punched right through the cushioning.

Then the custom orthotics. Three hundred dollars, molded to my arch.

Same result, more expensive. They worked right up until I took them off at the door. Then the first step inside split my heel open again.

Then stretching, because half the internet is convinced tight calves are the whole story.

Every morning and every night. The wall stretch, the towel pull, calf raises off the bottom stair. My calves got looser. I could reach further than I had in years.

My heel didn't notice. Three weeks, no change. Six weeks, no change. Ten weeks, no change.

Then the massage gun, every night, on those same calves.

Twenty minutes a night for months. It felt good while I did it. My calves felt worked on, looser, warmer. And the next morning my heel greeted me exactly the same way it always did.

The frozen water bottle. Every night until my heel went numb.

The cold quieted the burning while the cold was there. Twenty minutes after I dried my foot off, the stabbing came back, angrier for having been interrupted.

The night splint. Eight hours of my foot held stretched.

I gave the whole thing back in one second, on the first step of the morning.

Cortisone. Twice, at the clinical dose.

Quiet for a few weeks, then the slow return, and the appointment for the next one already in my calendar.

Two podiatrists. One ultrasound that showed thickening, which sounded serious and told me nothing about what to actually do.

Some of it helped for a day or two.

Then that pain always came back.

Two and a half years of that.

At some point I stopped believing any of it was going to work.

And one night I found myself thinking back through the whole two and a half years, everything I'd done, trying to find any pattern at all.

Three things didn't fit the story I'd been told.

One. Six weeks of complete rest made it worse. Not neutral. Worse.

Two. There were days I was on my feet constantly, running errands all afternoon, and I woke up the next morning better than usual. I never understood why.

Three. Every single thing that ever helped, only helped for a while. The ice. The stretching. Even the shot.

Not one of them ever lasted.

Everything I'd been told said rest heals it and load damages it.

My own two and a half years said something else entirely.

That's when I stopped researching plantar fasciitis and started researching why a heel might not heal.

And somewhere down in a thread, I found a comment from a woman who said her heel finally healed once she fixed her circulation.

Her circulation.

Two and a half years of reading. Stretches, shoes, insoles, splints, shots. Every single thing pointed at the foot.

This was the first thing I had ever read that pointed somewhere else.

I booked an appointment with a circulation doctor. A real physician who specializes in it. Not another foot doctor.

She let me talk all the way through without interrupting.

I told her all of it. The two and a half years. Everything I'd tried. And the part that had never made sense to me. That I rested it completely for six weeks, and it got worse.

She nodded.

"That's not strange. That's actually the answer."

Then she pulled over a notepad and drew a foot, and a line running up the back of the leg.

"Here's what nobody explained to you. The bottom of your foot is just about the hardest place in your whole body for blood to reach. It's the farthest point from your heart. And it's the one place where blood has to climb straight back up, against GRAVITY, to get out."

"Okay," I said.

"What makes that climb happen is a muscle deep in your calf. It's called the soleus. Some people call it the second heart. Every time it squeezes, it pushes the blood out of your feet and back up your legs."

"My calf? But the pain is in my heel."

"Stay with me. How many hours a day are you at that desk?"

"Nine."

"For how many years?"

"Close to twenty."

"That's what stacked up. That muscle stiffens the longer it spends not moving, and it does it a little more every year. By the time you hit your forties, yours had been stiffening long enough to stop."

"Once it stiffens, it can't push the blood back up anymore. So the old blood just sits down there in your foot. Pooling. Going nowhere. We call it stagnant blood."

"And as long as that old blood is sitting there, fresh blood can't get in behind it. It can't reach your heel at all."

"So it was never the plantar fascia."

"Think about what that means," she said. "Every step you take opens tiny damage in your heel. That's normal. That's just what walking is. In most people, it heals overnight."

"Mine doesn't."

"Healing takes oxygen. Oxygen rides in on fresh blood. And fresh blood isn't reaching your heel. So this morning, your first step came down on damage that never healed. And tore it open again."

She let that sit there a second.

"Torn open. Never healed. Torn open again. Every morning. That's the stabbing."

"So the running was making it worse."

"You were opening more damage than most people ever do, with less ability to heal it than most people have. That's the whole picture."

"Then why didn't running fix the muscle? I did it for twenty years."

"Because by the time this started, it was already too stiff for that. Once it's there, normal movement isn't enough to bring it back. That's the point you were already past."

"And the six weeks of rest?"

"You added six more weeks of not moving to a muscle that was already stiffening from exactly that. You weren't resting it. You were speeding it up."

I want you to understand what that did to me, sitting in that chair.

Two and a half years of doing exactly what I was told, and the thing I'd been told was the single most damaging thing I did.

"Then why didn't the massage gun work? I've been on those calves every night for two years."

"On the surface," she said. "The muscle you can reach with a massage gun or a stretch is the one on top. The soleus sits underneath it. You can't get to it by pressing from the outside. It has to contract."

Then I said the thing I'd been holding since I sat down.

"I've spent thousands of dollars on shoes and insoles."

"Every insole you've ever bought sits under your foot," she said. "The reason your heel can't heal is above it."

I sat there going back through everything I'd tried.

Every single thing on that list was aimed at the part that hurt. Not one of them had ever gone anywhere near the reason the blood stopped reaching my heel in the first place.

I asked her how to get it working again.

"You have to make it squeeze. Directly. In the clinic we use EMS for that. Electrical stimulation, at a frequency that goes deep enough to reach the soleus. It makes the muscle contract on its own, without you standing, without you moving."

"The contractions loosen it, and the pump starts working again. The stagnant blood finally moves out, fresh blood gets in, and the damage in your heel starts getting the oxygen it needs. It starts healing for the first time in years."

"Do I have to keep coming here?"

"There are home units now. But listen, because this part matters. If it doesn't run at 40Hz, it's not reaching the soleus. It's just buzzing your skin. Most of what's out there is a massager with a fancy name. Check the frequency before you buy anything."

That night I sat at the kitchen table with my phone.

She was right. Page after page of foot massagers. Soothing vibration. Relaxing relief. Not one of them said what frequency they ran at.

Then I found one that did. A flat mat called FlowLab Revive. Right on the page: 40Hz EMS, built to reach the soleus. You sit in a chair, put your bare feet on it, fifteen minutes.

It had a 90-day money-back guarantee.

After everything that hadn't worked, one more try wasn't going to break me.

I ordered it.

Here's what happened, day by day.

Day 1. Fifteen minutes in my chair. My calves started squeezing on their own. Not painful. Deep. A slow grip way down in there, someplace the massage gun had never once reached.

When I stood up, it felt like maybe a little of it had lifted. I told myself it was probably nothing. I'd fooled myself before.

Day 3. The morning step was quieter. Not gone. But it didn't take my breath away. I didn't trust it.

Day 8. Crossed the bedroom before the ache caught up with me. Wasn't touching the wall. I stood in the doorway for a second working out what had just not happened.

Day 15. Walked two miles. Zero pain during. Mild irritation that evening, maybe a 1 out of 10. Gone by morning.

That "gone by morning" is the whole thing. That had not happened once in two and a half years.

Day 26. First step in the morning was just a step. Some mornings I forgot to brace for it entirely.

Week 6. Ran a mile. Slowly. Nothing that night. Nothing the next morning.

Week 10. Four miles. Zero.

Week 12. I've been running three days a week for the past month. I still do my fifteen minutes every night, sitting in the chair, while the TV is on. That's the entire routine.

I'm not going to tell you I'm 100% cured, because I don't know what my feet would do at mile twenty right now and I'm not going to find out this month.

But two and a half years of my life were organized around my heel, and now they aren't.

Here's what I need you to take from this.

If you've stretched and rolled and splinted and injected and none of it lasted, that wasn't you failing the treatment.

The treatment was failing you.

Every one of those things works on the part that hurts. Not one of them touches the muscle that decides whether blood ever gets down there at all.

And if you've been resting it and waiting, I need you to hear the thing that cost me the most.

Rest is not doing what you think it's doing. Nothing in your heel is healing while you sit still. It's only stacking.

That muscle gets a little stiffer every year, and every month, and every long weekend you spend on the couch waiting for it to calm down.

I lost two and a half years finding that out. The answer was in front of me the whole time. I just couldn't see what I was looking at.

I don't know how much time you've already lost.

How many plans you've given up.

How many mornings you've spent bracing before your foot even touches the floor, quietly wondering, will it hurt today.

But I know you get up and do the day anyway.

That's exactly why you need to know this.

That pain in your heel can be fixed.

Not managed. Not survived. Fixed.

The mat I use is called FlowLab Revive EMS. It was the only one I found that met the 40Hz the doctor told me about. You sit in your chair, you put your feet on it, fifteen minutes.

It comes with the same 90-day guarantee that got me to try it. If your first step isn't different, you send it back and get every dollar. They keep the risk. Not you.

The site I ordered mine from is linked below.

Don't wait until you start hating yourself for it, like I did.

I'm 51. I saw a podiatrist, an orthopedic surgeon, and a rheumatologist. Not one pressed on my heel.

The podiatrist sent me for X-rays. Clean. The surgeon ordered an ultrasound and blood work. The ultrasound showed the band under my heel was thickened, and they said that confirmed the diagnosis. The blood work for rheumatoid arthritis and thyroid came back normal.

"Everything looks fine," the surgeon said. "It's plantar fasciitis. It's common at this age, and we've ruled out everything else."

Clean tests. Three specialists. And every single morning my feet refused to hold me up without pain.

I was 46 when the first doctor said "plantar fasciitis," and for five years I did everything they told me to do.

I stretched my calves against the doorframe every morning before I was allowed to take a step. I rolled a frozen water bottle under my foot every night for ten minutes of relief that was gone by the time I stood up.

They told me to try shoes. So I bought the Hokas, then the Brooks, then Birkenstocks, then Oofos slides for the house, then a pair of Vionics.

They told me to try insoles. So I bought Dr. Scholl's inserts, then Superfeet, then a night splint, then the Strassburg sock.

The podiatrist said custom orthotics would fix it in a month. I paid $500, insurance wouldn't cover them, and within two weeks they'd given me nerve pain in both feet.

They gave me a cortisone shot. It worked for about four weeks, and I wore sandals on holiday like a normal person. Then it wore off, and it took the sandals with it.

After that came the walking boot, the Epsom soaks, the acupuncture. Every new appointment, same answer. "It's plantar fasciitis. Losing a few pounds would help."

I tried losing the pounds, and it cost me two weeks of worse pain. When my hips started aching too I got the HRT patch, and it took the hip ache and the hot flashes and left my feet exactly where they were.

I felt like I was making it up. The tests were clean and the doctors weren't worried, and every morning at 5:40 I still put my hand flat on the wall before my foot touched the floor. That first step felt like someone had caned my feet in the night.

By 10am I'd be standing at the front desk of the vet clinic where I work, concrete floor, first two Advil down. By 2pm the bottoms of my feet were the worst part of me. It felt like walking on marbles, like there was nothing between my bones and the concrete.

And while the doctors kept not finding anything wrong, my life kept getting smaller.

I stopped walking anywhere I didn't have to. Put on thirty pounds because I couldn't walk more than a mile.

My husband went out for his evening walk alone. I'd told him to stop asking me to come. When he stopped asking, that was worse. Two years earlier we'd climbed a mountain on our anniversary, and now I could hardly climb the stairs to bed.

Last spring I went on vacation with my parents, who are almost 80, and they zoomed around the whole week while I kept taking breaks for my feet. On the day everyone hiked out to the waterfall, I stayed at the hotel.

bodyText:
I used to golf every weekend for 12 years, I haven't touched a club in 4 years because of plantar fasciitis, last week I did 18 holes because I learned what recovery actually needs.

I'm 56. I had this in my right foot for a little over four years.

Four years is the part I need you to sit with. Because everything you read about plantar fasciitis tells you it takes a few months. Rest it, stretch it, give it time, it heals. Mine never healed. Four years and it never once healed, and for a long time I thought there was something wrong with me specifically.

The mornings. That first step out of bed is the one that tells you what kind of day it's going to be. I'd sit on the edge of the mattress and look at the floor and work up to it. Some mornings I'd hold the dresser and put my heel down in stages, like an old man, and I did not want to be an old man. 

Then it stopped being just mornings. It was standing long enough to make coffee. It was walking to get the mail. It was Sunday, which used to be dad cooking steaks on the grill. That turned into me getting the grill going and then handing the tongs to my son and going to sit down. He didn't say anything about it. I know he was just trying to help me out but he’s my son, I should be helping him. 

But the golf is what actually broke my heart.

Twelve years, every weekend, same group of guys. That was my thing. That was the week paying off. And there's no faking your way through eighteen holes. That's four hours on your feet, a good five miles of walking.  I tried to keep going for a while. I'd take the cart. 

But you can't hide it in your swing. I couldn't load that foot without it lighting up, so I babied it, and my game fell apart. I went from hanging with anyone in the group to apologizing on every tee. And then one Saturday on about the sixth hole I couldn't put weight on it to swing, and I told the guys I'd wait in the clubhouse, and I sat there and watched them finish through the window.

I didn't go back. I told them my foot was acting up and I'd see them when it settled down. It didn't settle down. Weekends came and went and after a while they stopped asking, and that was the part that got me. That my spot just closed over.

I did everything they tell you.

Two podiatrists. Custom orthotics, the three hundred dollar kind. Store inserts before those. Stretches every morning, the calf one against the wall, the towel pull. The frozen water bottle. A night splint I slept in like a fool for months. New shoes, the cushioned ones everybody online swears by. And a cortisone shot I was scared of that helped for a few weeks and then came back worse than before.

Four years of doing everything right and it never moved.

The second podiatrist was the one who said surgery. Said we'd tried everything else and the next step was cutting the fascia to release it. She said it like I was out of options. I wasn't ready to let anyone cut into my foot on the last idea they had, so I found another doctor.

I was expecting to hear the same thing, but I guess I wanted to hear it one more time from someone else before I commit to it. 

The man I saw had been doing feet for twenty years. He watched me walk. He asked how long, and I said four years, and he stopped writing and looked at me.

He said, "Four years? Then no one ever fixed the actual problem, because this isn't supposed to last four years."

I said I know it's not, believe me, I've read everything.

He said, "Then let me tell you why it never healed. Because I promise you nobody has."

Here it is.

When this starts, it's an overload injury. You get tiny tears in the fascia. Your body sends inflammation, because that's what a body does when something tears. That part's normal. That's the repair crew showing up.

The problem is the repair crew never gets to finish the job.

Because you can't stop using your foot. You have to stand at the sink. You have to walk to the bathroom. So the tissue gets torn again before it's done healing from the last time, and again every time you take a step, and it never once completes a repair.

And a tissue that never finishes a repair doesn't stay the same. It changes. The fibers that are supposed to lie down straight and tight, like the strands of a rope, come back tangled and weak. The rope stops being a rope and turns into frayed cord.

It stops being an injury and becomes damage that just sits there, and every step you take makes it a little worse.

That's why four years. It was never healing. I'd been treating it like a wound that needed time, and time was the one thing that was making it worse, because every day was another day of tearing.

Then he told me the two things that healing actually needs, and why I'd never given my foot either one.

The first is a break from the tearing. The load has to come off fascia enough that it stops getting ripped open every step. Everything I'd tried cushioned the ground. None of it took the load off the tissue itself.

The second is blood. He said the reason this tissue heals so slowly, the reason it's stubborn in everybody, is that it sits at the very bottom of your foot, farthest from your heart, and it barely gets any blood. Blood is what rebuilds tissue. A part of the body that can't get blood can't heal, no matter how long you wait.

And that's when four years of failure rearranged themselves in front of me. He told my they all helped short term, but nothing resulted in healing. 

I thought the first step hurt because the foot stiffened overnight. It's worse than that. At night, off your feet, your body finally starts trying to patch that tissue. But there's almost no blood reaching it while you lie still, so the patch it builds is thin. Then you stand up in the morning and your full weight comes down and tears it right back open. That first step is you ripping apart the little bit of repair you got overnight.

The stretches. I was pulling on frayed cord every morning and calling it treatment.

The orthotics and the shoes. They cushioned the landing and propped the arch from underneath. They never took the load off the tissue and they never brought it any blood. A pillow under a wound.

The cortisone. An anti inflammatory, aimed at inflammation, and I learned after 4 weeks the inflammation wasn't even the problem anymore. It quieted things for a few weeks while the cord frayed on.

None of it failed because I did it wrong. All of it failed because not one of those things did either of the two things my foot actually needed to recover.

I asked him why nobody had told me this in four years.

He was honest. He said the first line treatments are the first line treatments, and for most people they work, and those people get better and everyone moves on. The ones who don't get better keep coming back and get the next thing on the list, and then the shot, and then the talk about surgery. He said there's no money in telling a man his tissue just needs the load off and some blood. There's money in the injection.

So I asked him what does that, then.

He opened a drawer and put something in my hand.

It was a sleeve. Like a thick sock with the toes open, a couple of straps across the middle. Thin enough to disappear inside a shoe. I remember thinking, four years and two podiatrists and the answer is a sock.

He told me he didn't learn this in a classroom. He learned it watching men like me come back a third and fourth time after everything else failed. And once he understood what the tissue actually needed, he started sending people to this instead of to the next shot.

He said the straps hold the arch and take the load off the fascia, so it finally stops getting torn with every step, even while you're walking around all day. And the compression drives blood down into the tissue that's been starved for years.

I'll be honest, I still didn't believe it. I had a list and years full of things that didn't work.

I put it on that night when I got home.

It goes on like a sock. You pull the straps snug across the arch and you feel them take hold, like a hand pushing the bottom of your foot from underneath.

And I stood up and put my weight on it, braced for the usual.

It wasn't gone. I want to be straight about that. But it wasn't pain that stops you, the kind that has you reaching for a railing. It was a dull version of it. I stood in my kitchen and put my weight down again on purpose, just to check, because I didn't trust it.

Two days later I walked to the kitchen in the morning without leaning on anything. I just walked. I said "how bout that" out loud to nobody.

Three weeks in I cooked my steaks standing flat on both feet the whole time. Daddy’s steaks were back.

And then came the day I found out it was real. The sleeve was in the wash and I had a day at home with nothing to put on, and I figured fine, one day. By the afternoon I felt it coming back up through my heel. But it was nothing like before. A low ache, the kind a bruise gives you. And I realized two things sitting at my kitchen table. This is the best my foot felt in four years. And I hadn't thought about my feet in three weeks. Until I didn’t wear it for 1 day.

bodyText:
I was diagnosed with plantar fasciitis at 46. I'm 51 now. Turns out that was never what was wrong with my feet.

For five years I "managed" a diagnosis that was only ever half the story.

At 46 I was hiking most weekends and walking with my husband every evening after dinner. By 47 my whole life had shrunk to whatever my feet would allow that day, and the doctors kept telling me the feet were the whole problem.

By the time my alarm went off at 5:40, I already knew what the first step was going to feel like. I'd swing my legs over the side and put my hand flat on the wall before my foot touched the floor. That first step felt like someone had caned my feet in the night.

By 10am I'd be standing at the front desk of the vet clinic where I work, concrete floor, first two Advil down. Still nothing.

By 2pm the bottoms of my feet were the worst part of me. It felt like walking on marbles, like there was nothing between my bones and the concrete.

And the math never stopped. If I walked the dog to the end of the street and back, I was done for the night.

I stopped walking anywhere I didn't have to, and took up the exercise bike in the garage instead, and put on thirty pounds because I couldn't walk more than a mile.

My husband still went out for his walk every evening after dinner. I watched him go from the couch, same spot, and two years earlier we'd climbed a mountain on our anniversary and now I could hardly climb the stairs to bed.

I'd told him to stop asking me to come. When he stopped asking, that was worse.

Last spring I went on vacation with my parents, who are almost 80, and they zoomed around the whole week while I kept taking breaks for my feet. On the day everyone hiked out to the waterfall, I stayed at the hotel.

I wanted to be out with the dog, cooking, even cleaning the house. Instead I was on the couch, because even standing hurt, and I hadn't seen my friends in months because everything they did involved walking.

I looked fine on the outside. Inside, every part of my life was getting smaller, and my feet were the reason for all of it.

And every doctor just nodded. "That's plantar fasciitis. It's an age thing, and losing a few pounds would help."

Five years of stretching my calves against the doorframe before I was allowed to take a step. Five years of rolling a frozen water bottle under my foot every night for ten minutes of relief that was gone by the time I stood up. I did everything they asked.

I bought the Hokas, then the Brooks, then Birkenstocks, then Oofos slides for the house, then a pair of Vionics. After the shoes came the Dr. Scholl's inserts, then Superfeet, then a night splint, then the Strassburg sock.

I paid $500 for custom orthotics that insurance wouldn't cover, because the podiatrist swore they'd fix it in a month. Within two weeks they'd given me nerve pain in both feet every time I put them on.

The cortisone shot helped for about four weeks, and I wore sandals on holiday like a normal person. Then it wore off, and it took the sandals with it.

Then they sent me to a specialist. Podiatrist first, then an orthopedic surgeon, then a rheumatologist, eight months of appointments in all.

The X-rays were clean. The ultrasound showed the band under my heel was thickened, which they said just confirmed the diagnosis, and the blood work for rheumatoid arthritis and thyroid came back normal.

"Everything looks fine," the surgeon said. "It's plantar fasciitis. It's common at this age, and we've ruled out everything else."

I felt like I was making it up. The tests were clean and the doctors weren't worried, and every single morning my feet refused to hold me up without pain.

I tried losing the pounds, and it cost me two weeks of worse pain. When my hips started aching too I got the HRT patch, and it took the hip ache and the hot flashes and left my feet exactly where they were.

After that came the walking boot, the Epsom soaks, the acupuncture. Nothing worked, and every season there was one more thing I didn't do anymore.

I started to believe this was just my life now. That I'd spend the rest of it watching everyone else go while I planned my whole day around my feet. It felt like the next step was crutches, and after that my life was basically over.

Then my neighbor asked me a question no podiatrist ever had. She's a nurse at a foot and ankle clinic. We were standing in her driveway and I was telling her I couldn't get through the grocery store anymore without sitting in the car for twenty minutes after, and that I'd just cancelled the hiking trip we'd booked a year ago.

"Has anyone ever actually pressed on your heel and checked how much padding is left under it?"

I almost laughed. "I've tried insoles and I've tried orthotics, and they didn't do anything."

She shook her head. "That's not what I asked. Press your thumb into the middle of your heel."

I did, standing there in her driveway, and it was bone, right under the skin.

"Ten years ago there was a thick pad of fat there," she said. "It's your body's shock absorber. Every step you've ever taken landed on it."

"You're telling me I'm missing fat off the bottom of my feet?"

"I'm telling you that plantar fasciitis was never the real problem. It's what happens when the pad goes."

"Your heel bone hits the floor about 8,000 times a day. With the pad there, that gets spread out. With the pad gone, all of it lands on one hard point, and that hammering is what keeps the band under your heel inflamed."

"Overnight it starts to heal. Then your first step in the morning lands bone on floor and rips it open again. That's why you hold the wall."

"What would even cause that?"

"It thins as your hormones shift. From your mid-30s on, and women's pads are thinner than men's to begin with. Your weight didn't do this, and neither did your shoes."

She looked at me. "Your life didn't get smaller because there's anything wrong with you. One part wore out, and nobody warned you."

"Once it's gone, it doesn't grow back. Researchers call it fat pad atrophy, and it keeps your heel landing on bone even on the days you rest it, even after the stretches, even when the X-ray comes back clean."

"The band was sore because the bone was hammering it. You've spent five years treating the sore part and nothing under it."

"That first step in the morning, after a full night of sleep? That's not plantar fasciitis. That's your heel bone hitting the floor with nothing between them."

"And the marbles feeling?"

"Same thing. Pain is weight on a small spot, and comfort is the same weight spread over a big area. You can lie on a bed of nails, but you can't lie on one nail."

"But I've tried insoles," I said.

"You tried half the job," she said. "A fix has to do two jobs at once: put a real pad between the bone and the floor, and spread your weight across the whole foot so the bone doesn't carry it all. Everything you bought did one or the other."

"Drugstore inserts are the soft part, badly. A few millimetres of foam, and your bare heel squashes it flat on the first step. Your custom orthotics were the spreading part, hard plastic straight under a bare bone, which is why they hurt."

"Half the job feels like nothing."

I stared at her. Five years, three specialists, every test coming back clean, and nobody had ever pressed on my heel.

I went home and Googled "heel fat pad thinning women" and fell into a rabbit hole. Foot and ankle journals describing the pad under the heel thinning with age and hormone changes.

Everything she said checked out.

I texted her the next morning. "Okay, say you're right. What do I actually do?"

She called on her lunch break. "The pad doesn't grow back, so you put one under your foot from the outside. You need two parts in one insole."

"A thick pad under the heel and the front of the foot, thick enough that a bare heel can't flatten it. And a firm cradle under the arch that catches part of every step, so the heel never carries the whole load alone."

"Soft where you're bare, firm where you're not. Your heel stops hammering, and the band finally gets a rest that lasts past the first step."

"And it has to go in the slippers by your bed. The first step of the day is the one that does the damage, and your Hokas are by the front door at 5:40 in the morning."

"I keep a pair in my own slippers. We started telling patients about them last year."

This sounded too simple to me. But I'd been dragging myself through every day for five years. "Where do I get one?"

"You can't grab any insole off the shelf," she said. "Most of them are either thin foam or a hard shell, and the thick ones flatten out in a month."

"The one I use is Rebloom. It's a thick foam base under the heel and the front of the foot, with a firm arch cradle built into it, and you trim it to fit. It's the only one I've found that does both."

I looked it up that night. There was a 90-day money-back guarantee. After five years of shoes and shots and specialists that failed, what was one more try?

They came in four days, and I put them straight into the slippers by my bed. The first morning I still put my hand on the wall out of habit, and the step still hurt. Like ten percent less.

By day four, I got to the bathroom without touching the wall, and stood there with my hand up in the air where the wall should have been.

By the end of week one I moved them into my work sneakers and got through a full shift on that concrete without my afternoon Advil. I'd forgotten to take it.

Since spring I'd been keeping a list on my phone of how far I could walk before my feet quit. By the end of week two, it was around the block twice with no sitting in between. Nearly triple what I'd managed all year.

Then came week three. I woke up before my alarm, lay in the quiet, and waited for it. The caned feeling, the marbles, that first-step pain that had met me every single morning for five years.

It wasn't there. I put my foot down and it held, and for the first time in five years the word for it wasn't "manageable." It was fine.

For the first time in five years, I walked barefoot across my kitchen tile to make coffee and didn't think about my feet until the coffee was done.

That Saturday I walked the dog to the end of the street and back and kept going, and got through the whole day without planning it around my feet.

For the first time in five years, my husband put his shoes on for his walk and I put mine on too. Halfway around the block he looked at me and said "you're walking like yourself again."

Two weekends later I did the trail behind the reservoir, the one I hadn't touched in four years. Three miles, and I sat in the car afterward and cried, and for once it wasn't from pain.

Five years of trails and evening walks and trips I sat out, and the whole time it was never my life that had to get smaller. It was a pad.

I don't have a plantar fasciitis problem. I never did. And my life was never over, either.

What I'd had was five years of a missing pad, my heel hitting the floor with nothing between them, and a sore band taking the blame.

And not one person in a white coat thought to press on my heel.

I still wear the patch, and I still do the stretches out of habit. The concrete at work hasn't changed either. But now there's a pad under my heel before my foot touches the floor.

Every morning my feet go straight into the slippers with the pad in them, and at work they go into my sneakers. There's nothing to take and nothing to do, and it takes as long as putting on shoes.

That should be the first thing anyone tells a woman whose feet started hurting in her 40s.

If you've been told you have plantar fasciitis… If you've done the stretches and the shots and the orthotics and nothing has stuck…

If your X-rays and your blood work keep coming back clean… If you wake up after eight hours of sleep and put your hand on the wall before your foot touches the floor…

If you've stopped saying yes to the walk, the market, the vacation… If your world has shrunk to whatever your feet will allow that day…

I'm not saying you're definitely missing the pad under your heel. But I spent five years treating a sore band while the real problem got worse every single day, and five years watching my life get smaller every season over one part that had simply worn out.

Rebloom is a small company that makes one thing.

Right now they're running a sale. I checked the site this morning and ordered a second pair, so I can stop moving one pair back and forth between the slippers and my work shoes.

They have a 90-day money-back guarantee. Three full months to find out if it works for you. If nothing changes, you get your money back.

But if it works? If the first morning that step lands on padding instead of bone, even just a little?

If by week one you get to the bathroom without touching the wall? If a month from now you put your shoes on for the evening walk and go the whole way, and the weekend after that you're back on a trail?

You'll wish you'd started five years ago. I know I do. I took all of it for granted.

bodyText:
I paid four different podiatrists to look at the same foot over ten years, and I could have saved the money by recording the first one.

Wider shoes. Ibuprofen on the bad days. Bunions are progressive. Monitor. When it is bad enough, we talk about surgery.

I am 62. I ran an elementary school outside Cleveland for thirty-four years and I know what it sounds like when someone reads from a script. By the fourth appointment the script had a date on it: April, six to twelve weeks non-weight-bearing, seventy to eighty percent of patients happy, one in four bunions back within a few years. He was decent about it. He said we had missed the window for anything conservative. I booked it.

Then my neighbor, who is a physical therapist and has never once looked at my feet professionally, watched me pull my clogs off in my kitchen and asked whether anyone had walked me through the soft tissue side of this.

Nobody had. In ten years, four foot specialists, nobody.

Here is what she told me, and I have thought about it every day since. The big toe is held in place by a capsule of tendon and ligament around the joint. Load that capsule wrong for long enough, in narrow shoes, with a walking pattern that has been compensating for years, and one side tightens while the other stretches. The tissue slowly settles into a new shape. The bone has no choice but to follow, because the bone is anchored by the tissue and not the other way round.

The bump is not a growth. It is the head of a bone I was born with, dragged sideways by tissue that was trained wrong for thirty years.

Four doctors had treated that as a bone problem. Treat it as a bone problem and there is exactly one tool left, and it is a saw. Treat the tissue and it is a different conversation, one nobody had bothered to have with me because, as she put it, surgery has a billing code and a talk about connective tissue does not.

She told me why the night splint I wore for two years did nothing: eight hours of pulling in bed against sixteen hours of shoes pushing the other way. She told me the tissue only changes when the foot is carrying weight, so what matters is what is on your foot while you walk, not while you sleep. And she told me to try a sleeve-anchored aligner for three months before April. If it helped I would know. If it did not, the surgery would still be there.

I cancelled April. Ten months in, the angle on my X-ray has come back a few degrees and a day of errands hurts about half what it did. The bunion is still there. I am not selling you a new foot.

What I am angry about is the decade. At 51 or 53, when the joint was still moderate, nobody gave me a single thing to do except wait for it to get worse.

I wrote the whole thing down, including what she said about which bunions still respond and how long it takes. Read it before your next appointment. That appointment goes differently once you have.

You've got the pile to show for it. The frozen bottle. A drawer full of insoles. The night splint too bulky to sleep in. Every one of them was a "maybe this is the one."

The band under your foot keeps going past your heel. It's part of a web of fascia that runs up your leg, all the way to your hip.

Somewhere up there, that web has glued down. Where it's stuck is called an adhesion. You can't feel it where it sits, so nobody thinks to look for it.

Every night it yanks the band tight again and wipes out whatever helped that day.

It's why an X-ray looks fine, too. X-rays show bone. Fascia and adhesions don't show up at all.

And it won't let go on its own. Tonight it'll be dragging on your heel again, from one of three spots nobody checks. None of them are where it hurts.
