bodyText:
I'm a podiatrist. I've made custom orthotics for thousands of kids over 35 years. Last month I refused to make a pair for my own son.

I want to explain why. Because there is a sentence I have never once said out loud in an exam room in 35 years.

Nobody told me I couldn't say it. There's no rule. I just never said it, because I'm the one who makes the orthotics.

I'm not staying quiet about it anymore.

My name is Dr. Blane. I've run a small podiatry practice for most of my adult life. A big part of what walks through my door is a mom and a kid somewhere between seven and thirteen, and the kid is limping.

Usually it's a soccer kid. Sometimes basketball, sometimes dance. The mom says he's complaining after practice, or he's asking to sit out, or she's noticed his ankles roll inward when he runs. Almost always she's been told it's growing pains by somebody before me.

Here's what happens next, and I've done it thousands of times.

I have him stand on the plate. The scan comes up on the screen and I turn it toward his mom. She sees the arch flattened out and the pressure sitting on the inside of the foot, and her face changes, because now it's real.

I take a mold of his feet. Three weeks later the customs come in. I slide one into his sneaker, he stands up, and the foot sits perfectly. Held right where it should be. Mom sees it. She pays somewhere around $450, because insurance almost never covers it.

And I say the thing I've said thousands of times.

"He'll grow. Let's see you back in six months."

Six months later they're back. His foot grew. The customs don't fit anymore. And the limp is the same limp.

That's when Mom says it, a little embarrassed, looking at the floor instead of me.

"Honestly, he hasn't really been wearing them."

And I nod. And I measure him for the next pair.

I've heard every version of it. He pulls them out at halftime because they dig in. They're in last year's sneakers, not the cleats he actually plays in. They're at the bottom of the soccer bag under wet socks. One dad brought a pair back still in the box.

Every scan on my screen looked perfect. Every foot in my office sat exactly where I put it.

And the kid was still limping to the car.

The first few years you tell yourself it's the parents not enforcing it. Or the kid being difficult. By year ten you stop telling yourself stories. By year fifteen you start keeping a drawer.

I started that drawer in 2009. It's the bottom drawer in my exam room, and it's full of outgrown custom orthotics that parents brought back hoping I could resize them. I can't. A custom is molded to one foot at one moment, and a nine-year-old's foot is a different foot by spring.

I'm not going to tell you how many pairs are in there. It would sound like I'm making it up.

I want to be honest about something before I go further, because you might be reading this thinking I'm some kind of hero for saying it.

I'm not. I've made a lot of money making custom orthotics. Millions of dollars over 35 years, if I'm being honest with you. It paid for my practice, my staff, and my house.

I'm not going to call custom orthotics a scam, because they're not. When one is in the shoe, it does exactly what it's built to do.

But nobody in that exam room measures the wearing. Not me, not the mom, not anyone. I get paid the day the orthotic is made. I get paid again six months later when it's outgrown. Whether it spent those six months inside a cleat or inside a bag has never once shown up on an invoice.

That's not corruption. It's just a business that gets paid on the fitting, not on the wearing. And I was very good at fitting.

That was the deal I made for 35 years.

Last month the deal blew up.

My son is nine. He plays soccer three days a week and he'd play seven if we let him. He came off the field on a Thursday and sat down on the curb with his cleats still on, and he didn't get up when the other kids ran to the parking lot.

I asked him what was going on.

"Dad, my feet hurt after every practice now."

Not once. Every practice. And I'm a podiatrist, and I hadn't noticed.

That night I had him walk across the kitchen floor in his socks while I sat on the tile and watched. Both ankles rolling inward with every step. The inside of his heel taking the landing. I have seen it thousands of times on other people's kids, and I'd never sat on my own floor and looked.

Saturday I brought him to the office and stood him on the plate. The scan came up. The same flattened arch. The same pressure on the inside edge. I've seen that exact picture more times than I can count.

The next step is the easiest thing in the world for me. I have the mold kit in the next room. I have the order form in the drawer above the one full of outgrown orthotics.

I sat at my desk with that form and I did not fill it in.

Because I knew exactly what was coming. I'd watched it thousands of times. The customs would come in. They'd sit perfectly on the plate. And by October I'd be finding them at the bottom of his soccer bag, and he'd be sitting on that curb again, and I'd be looking at the same scan of a foot that had grown out of a $450 prop it never wore.

I drove home and my wife asked what was wrong. I told her I couldn't do it. She's been married to a podiatrist for a long time. She didn't argue.

That week is when everything changed for me.

I did what I hadn't done since residency. I sat down and actually read. Not the catalogs from the orthotic labs. Not the sales reps. The studies on kids' feet, the ones I'd stopped keeping up with somewhere around year ten because I thought I already knew the answer.

And I understood something I now can't believe I didn't understand.

What the foot looks like in my office was never the thing that mattered.

I want to say that again, because it took me most of that week to accept it. What the foot looks like in my office was never the thing that mattered. What the foot is doing on a field at 4:30 on a Tuesday is the thing that mattered.

I'd been treating the scan. I'd never treated the Tuesday.

Here's what's actually going on inside a kid like mine, in plain English.

The arch is supposed to work like a spring. It flexes when the foot lands and pushes back when the foot pushes off. That's how a kid runs for two hours and comes home tired but fine.

When the arch rolls inward, that spring gives out under load. The foot lands and just keeps collapsing. The heel takes the hit from a bad angle. The muscles and tissue along the inside of the foot get pulled with every single step, and a nine-year-old at soccer practice takes thousands of steps.

That pull, over and over, is the ache my son was feeling on the curb.

And it doesn't stay in the foot. The ankle has to follow the foot. The knee has to follow the ankle. A study of 92,000 adolescents found that kids with moderate to severe flat feet had nearly double the rate of knee pain and low back pain compared to kids with normal arches. That's association, not proof of cause, and I'll be careful to say so. But it's not nothing.

The one that stopped me cold was a 2025 study on school-aged kids specifically. Kids with flat feet scored about 42 percent higher on a standard pain scale than their classmates. And they were measurably less physically active.

Read that second part again. They hurt more, so they move less.

That's the curb. That's "can I sit out today." That's every mom in my office who said her son used to love practice.

I had those numbers on my wall for years. I'd never once thought about what they meant on a Tuesday.

Now I'm going to tell you what a custom orthotic actually does, because I had to sit with this myself before I could admit it.

A custom orthotic is a brace. It holds the foot in a position. When it's in the shoe, the arch is held up and the roll is reduced. That's real, and I've watched it help kids who wore them.

But it's a hard shell, and the reason it holds so well is the same reason a nine-year-old pulls it out. It doesn't flex when the foot flexes. Inside a tight cleat it presses and digs. Kids tell their moms it hurts more with it in, and I've heard that sentence in my exam room more times than I want to count.

So the kid stops wearing it. And when it's out of the shoe, nothing about that foot is any different than it was before I molded it. The brace did its job for exactly the hours it was in.

And even when it is in, holding a foot in place doesn't ask the muscles around the foot to do anything. It does the job for them.

Then the foot grows, and the $450 brace expires.

That's the machine I'd been running for 35 years. A prop that works when worn, that most kids won't wear, with a six-month shelf life. And a scan that looked perfect every single time.

I went through the rest of the menu that week too, the same way I'd heard parents go through it for decades.

Rest. Rest is free and every doctor says it first. It works, in the sense that the foot stops hurting because the foot stops running. Then he goes back to practice and the roll is exactly where it was, and the ache comes back with it. Rest, play, hurt, rest. Kids hate it and moms hate watching it.

Drugstore gel inserts. Soft, cheap, and my son would wear them. But there's no structure under the arch. A flat insert just follows the foot down as it collapses.

Supportive sneakers. Genuinely helpful for school. Useless the moment he laces up cleats, which is the exact moment his feet hurt.

Exercises on their own. This is the one that embarrassed me. Strengthening work is real and I know it's real. But it takes months to show up, and in the meantime the kid is on the curb tonight. And here's the part I have to own: in 35 years I had never once handed a family the exercises. I handed them the mold kit.

Every one of those options does one job. None of them do both.

That's the thing I finally saw sitting at my kitchen table with my son's scan on my laptop.

There are two different jobs here, and I'd been selling one of them as if it were the whole answer.

The first job is support during the hours that put the most load on the foot. Practice. Games. Recess. School hallways. And it only counts if it's in something a nine-year-old will actually keep in his cleat, because support sitting in a bag isn't supporting anything.

The second job is strengthening work outside the shoe. Simple, short, a few minutes a day, so the muscles around his feet and arches get asked to do something instead of being held the whole time. That's the part that makes it a plan for a growing kid instead of a prop with a shelf life.

Support while he plays. Work while he doesn't. And enough consistency that both actually happen.

I sat there thinking about that bottom drawer. Every pair in it was job one, done in a way the kid wouldn't tolerate, with job two never mentioned. Thousands of families paid me for half an answer, and I said "see you in six months" to every one of them.

That was the moment I stopped being a quiet podiatrist.

I wrote down what I'd actually want under my own son's foot, which I had never done in 35 years for anybody.

More structure under the arch than drugstore foam. Flexible enough to bend when his foot bends instead of fighting it. Soft enough on top that a nine-year-old forgets it's there. Cushioning under the heel, because that's where every landing starts. Thin enough to fit in a cleat. Cheap enough that when his foot grows in six months, replacing it isn't a decision. And something to go with it that actually gives him the exercises.

Then I did what a podiatrist does before trusting anything. I went and looked.

I found Footstr on a thread of soccer parents I'd never have read before that week. Moms comparing what their kids would and wouldn't keep in their shoes. Somebody had posted it with a sentence I'll never forget: "first pair he doesn't hate."

I read everything on the site the way I'd read a lab spec. It's soft on top with a structured, flexible support underneath the arch. It cushions the heel. It's built to help reduce the inward roll at the arch and ankle while the foot is in the shoe, without locking the foot in place like a hard shell. It's sized for kids and it fits in cleats. And it comes with a strengthening program, the exercises I'd never once handed anyone.

It comes as a four-pack. I understood why immediately. My son has cleats, school sneakers, indoor shoes, and the beat-up pair he wears everywhere else. One insole in one shoe would be support for a third of his day. Four pairs means it's just in his shoes, all of them, and nobody has to remember to move anything.

Four pairs cost less than the sales tax on one custom. I'll get to that.

I ordered them Saturday night. I did not fill in the order form.

I want to be honest about the first few days, because I know what parents want to hear and I'm not going to say it.

It wasn't anything.

He put them in his cleats before Tuesday practice and said "these are squishy" and ran off. That was the whole review. No miracle, no announcement.

Then the small things started.

WEEK 1: He finished Thursday practice without sitting down on the curb. He still said his feet were tired. But tired isn't hurt, and I've spent 35 years learning the difference.

WEEK 2: My wife pulled his cleats out of the bag to bang the mud off, and the insoles were still in them. Both of them. I've found thousands of customs in bags. I had never once found a support still in the shoe.

WEEK 3: We started the exercises. Five minutes on the living room rug after dinner, and I turned it into a contest so he'd do it. He beat me at the single-leg one and would not let it go. That was the first time in my career the strengthening part actually happened in a house.

WEEK 4: Tournament weekend. Two games Saturday, one Sunday. He played every minute of all three. On the drive home he asked if we could stop at the park. I said his feet must be exhausted. He said, "They're fine, why?"

WEEK 6: I brought him back to the office on a Saturday and stood him on the plate.

I'm not going to tell you the scan showed a brand new arch. It didn't. Six weeks doesn't rebuild a foot and I'd be lying to you if I said an insole does that. The roll was still there under load.

What was different is everything the scan can't see. He'd worn support every hour that mattered, without one argument. He'd done the work outside the shoe. And the limp I'd watched on my kitchen floor was gone.

I stood there looking at the screen, at the same picture I'd turned toward thousands of moms, and I did not reach for the order form.

And for the first time in 35 years, I didn't say "see you in six months."

There's no six-month appointment. When his foot grows, we open the next pair.

Monday morning a mom came in with her ten-year-old. Soccer. Limping after practice. Ankles rolling in when he walked down my hall. I stood him on the plate, turned the screen toward her, and she asked me the question I've been asked thousands of times.

"So which orthotic do you recommend?"

And I finally said the sentence.

"The orthotic I make is only as good as the hours your kid actually wears it. And most of them don't."

She just looked at me. Then she said, "Nobody's ever told me that."

I know. That's why I'm writing this.

I'm writing this because I can't keep doing it.

I can't keep turning a screen toward a mom, taking her $450, and saying "see you in six months" when I know where that orthotic is going to end up.

If your kid is coming off the field limping, or asking to sit out, or telling you his feet hurt after every practice now, and somebody has told you it's growing pains, I want you to read this twice. The pain isn't coming from nowhere. Kids with flat feet hurt more and move less, and it's measured. Your eyes aren't lying to you.

If you already paid for customs and you're finding them in the bag, you didn't fail. Your kid didn't fail. You were handed a brace built for a scan, not for a Tuesday. Support at the bottom of a soccer bag is supporting nothing.

If you've tried rest and gel inserts and better sneakers and your kid is still limping to the car, it's because each of those does one job. None of them does both.

Footstr. Four pairs, so it's in every shoe he actually plays in. Flexible support under the arch, cushioning under the heel, and the strengthening program to go with it. The thing I put under my own son's feet instead of the mold kit in the next room.

Right now the four-pack is $30.

I want to sit on that number for a second, because I've spent 35 years on the other side of it. A custom is $450. It expires every six months. That's $900 a year for a prop most kids pull out by halftime. Thirty dollars gets support into all four pairs of shoes at once, and when his foot grows, you open the next pack instead of scheduling the next appointment.

If your kid has practice this week, get it in his cleats before then. Every practice on a collapsed arch is another practice on the curb.

You don't have to be the mom in my exam room looking at the floor.

Dr. Blane, DPM, 35 years

P.S. I want to be clear about something. If your child has custom orthotics and actually wears them, and they're helping, keep them in his shoes. That's between you and your podiatrist and I'm not arguing with it. This letter is for the kid whose customs are in the bag. That's most of them. Nobody measured it, so nobody told you.

P.P.S. The exercises are the part I keep coming back to. Thirty-five years and I never handed a single family the strengthening work. Whatever you decide about the insoles, do the five minutes on the rug. Make it a contest. You'll lose the single-leg one.

bodyText:
I am going to say something that every parent who's watched their kid limp off a soccer field needs to hear.

It might not be growing pains.

It might be his feet.

I'm not a doctor. I'm a mom who spent almost a year telling my nine-year-old the same four words everyone kept telling me.

"You'll grow out of it."

What I finally noticed at a Tuesday practice is something I still can't stop thinking about.

Read every word of this before you let him quit.

My son is nine. He's played soccer since he was four. Last fall, a couple of months into the season, he started coming off the field holding his knee.

Just under the kneecap. Always the same spot.

At first it was only after games. Then it was after practice. Then it was on the walk from the field to the car.

I remember the exact night I stopped calling it a phase.

He came off the field slower than everyone else, one hand on his knee, cleats still tied when he sat down on the curb by the parking lot.

He didn't want help getting to the car. He just wanted to get there.

Normally the ride home is nonstop. Who scored. Who got yelled at. What he wants for dinner.

That night he was quiet until we hit our street.

Then he said, "Can you just tell coach I'm sick tomorrow?"

He wasn't sick.

He just didn't want to hurt again.

We'd already been to Dr. Reeves. He's been our family doctor since my son was three, and he was careful and kind and completely right.

"It's Osgood-Schlatter. Very common in active kids his age. His body's growing. Rest it, ice it, and he'll grow out of it."

So we did exactly that.

Ice after practice.
Stretching before bed.
Ibuprofen when it got bad.
A week off when it got really bad.

And to be fair...

rest worked.

That was the confusing part.

We'd pull him for a week and he'd stop limping. He'd tell me it felt fine. He'd be begging to go back by Thursday.

Then he'd go back, and within two or three practices we were right back on the curb by the parking lot.

Rest.
Better.
Return.
Pain.

Over and over.

I asked other parents. I asked his coach. I read every Reddit thread I could find at eleven at night.

Every single one said some version of what Dr. Reeves said.

He'll grow out of it.

And I wanted that to be enough. Honestly, I needed it to be enough, because it meant nothing was actually wrong and we just had to be patient.

But if rest was the whole answer, why did the pain come back every time he played?

One night after he'd gone inside I sat in the driveway with the engine off and typed an email to his coach.

"Hi, I think we're going to sit out the rest of the season."

I didn't send it. But I wrote it.

He was nine, and I was one click away from ending the thing he loved most because I didn't know what else to do.

The next practice, I did something I'd never once done in five years of soccer.

I stopped watching his knee.

I watched his feet.

And I saw it.

Every time he planted to change direction, his ankle rolled in underneath him. His arch flattened out against the inside of his cleat. Then he'd push off, and the whole leg would twist a little to catch up.

Not once. Every single stride.

I went home and pulled out his cleats. The inside edge of each one was worn down like someone had been sanding it.

His school shoes were the same. So were his sneakers.

I'd been looking at those shoes every day for months.

A few nights later I found a study that made it worse.

Researchers looked at more than 92,000 adolescents and found that kids with moderate to severe flat feet had nearly double the rate of anterior knee pain and intermittent low back pain compared to kids with normal arches.

Anterior knee pain. The front of the knee.

The exact spot my son grabs when he sits down on the curb.

Now, that study didn't say flat feet caused his Osgood-Schlatter. I'm not going to tell you it did.

But it wrecked one comforting assumption I'd been leaning on for a year.

That because he was nine, the way his feet moved couldn't really matter yet.

So I went back to Dr. Reeves. Not to argue. Just to ask.

"Could his feet have anything to do with this?"

And I'll never forget how honest he was about it.

"They could. When a kid comes in with knee pain, we look at the knee. That's where it hurts, so that's where we check. I don't usually have them take their shoes off."

Nobody was hiding anything from me.

The knee got all the attention because the knee was where it hurt.

Then he explained it in a way that finally made sense.

Every sprint, every cut, every landing starts at the ground. If the foot rolls in too far on every step, the ankle follows it, and the knee ends up working above that movement thousands of times every practice.

Osgood-Schlatter is already an irritation right where the tendon pulls on the growing bone below the kneecap. Extra strain from below doesn't help.

So we'd been resting the knee, and the knee would calm down.

Then he'd go back out on the same feet, doing the same thing, and the strain would start piling up again.

Rest treated where it hurt.

It didn't change what was happening underneath him.

That was the part I hadn't understood.

And look, some kids really do just grow out of it. I believe that.

But mine was limping every single week, and in a full year nobody, including me, had looked at his feet.

Dr. Reeves suggested support. Something under the arch to keep the foot from collapsing so far inward, especially during sports.

So we tried the thing everyone tries first.

Pharmacy inserts.

Soft, flat, twelve dollars. He said they felt "squishy." I watched him at the next practice and his foot rolled in exactly the same way. The foam just followed the collapse. It didn't give the arch anything to work against.

So we went the other direction.

Custom orthotics.

Appointment. Assessment. Casting. A three-week wait. About $400 by the time we walked out.

And to be completely fair...

they worked.

When he wore them, I could see the difference. His ankle stayed steadier when he planted.

For about a week I thought we were done.

Then I started finding them in the bottom of his soccer bag.

Under the shin guards. Under the dirty socks. One time, under half a sandwich.

They were hard. They were thick. They made his cleats feel a size too small. And he was nine, so "wear them anyway" lasted about as long as you'd expect.

$400 of support sitting in a bag, supporting nothing.

Four months later I got him to try them again and he pulled his foot right back out.

"They don't fit."

His feet had grown. Of course they had.

That's when I did the math on $400 twice a year for however many years it took.

And that's also when a different worry crept in. Even if I found something he'd actually wear, wasn't I just putting a cushion under the problem? What happens when he takes it out?

So I knew what I was looking for now.

Structured enough to keep his foot from collapsing.
Flexible enough that he'd forget it was there.
Cheap enough to replace when he outgrew it.
Something for school shoes, sneakers and cleats, so the support didn't stop when the shoes changed.

And some way for his feet to actually get stronger, not just get propped up.

I found Footstr in a parent thread. Another mom, another kid with knee pain, another soccer bag full of orthotics.

What made me actually order was that it had both halves.

The insole has a structured arch that flexes with the foot instead of locking it in a hard block. That was the exact middle ground between the foam that did nothing and the customs he refused to wear. It supports the inside of the arch, which is where his foot kept caving in, and helps reduce that excessive inward roll while he's moving.

There's cushioning under the heel, so every landing has a softer spot to start from instead of jarring straight up the leg.

It fits in regular shoes, sneakers and cleats. And it comes as a four pack for $30, which meant one pair in his school shoes, one in his sneakers, one in his cleats, and a spare for when he outgrew them.

Four pairs for less than a tenth of one custom orthotic.

And then the part I hadn't seen anywhere else.

It comes with a strengthening program. Short exercises he does at home, outside the shoe, for the muscles around his feet and arches.

The insole doesn't strengthen anything. It supports his foot during the hours that put the most demand on it. The exercises are the part that's meant to help his feet get stronger over time.

Support during activity. Strengthening work outside the shoe. Both, consistently.

For the first time, it felt like a plan instead of one more thing to do after he was already hurting.

Here's how it actually went.

WEEK 1:

I didn't watch his knee. I watched his bag. Every day I checked whether the insoles were still in his cleats.

They were. He never mentioned them once. That was the first sign, before anything else.

WEEK 2:

He finished a full practice. He still rubbed his knee a bit in the car, but he walked to the car instead of limping to it.

WEEK 4:

Saturday game, two halves, no curb. He jogged off the field with the rest of the team and asked if we could get food on the way home.

He'd stopped asking me to tell coach he was sick.

WEEK 6:

The ride home was nonstop again. Who scored, who got yelled at, what he wanted for dinner.

I couldn't get a word in.

I'm not going to tell you it cured his Osgood-Schlatter. It didn't. He still gets sore after a hard week. He still needs rest days.

But the loop broke. He's not going back onto the same collapsing feet every time the knee calms down.

And he's still playing.

I see the posts every week now.

"He limps after every practice but the doctor says it's just growing pains."

"Rest helps but it comes right back the second he plays again."

"She's nine and she asked to quit gymnastics. I don't know what to do."

"We spent $400 on orthotics and I found them in her backpack."

You didn't miss it.

Rest worked. The diagnosis was right. Everyone who told you he'd grow out of it was being honest with you.

That's exactly what made it so hard to see. When the answer works for a week, nobody keeps looking.

So here's the one thing I'd ask you to do.

Watch his feet at the next practice. Not the knee. The feet. Then look at the inside edge of his shoes.

If you see what I saw, put support under his arch and let him keep playing.

Slide the insoles into the shoes he already wears. Do the exercises with him at home. Then, before you watch his knee, watch his bag. If they're still in his cleats after a week, you're most of the way there.

I'm not promising you it fixes everything. I'm promising it's worth trying before you send the email I almost sent.

Four pairs for $30, here: https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

That's less than one copay. It's a fraction of one custom orthotic he might not wear.

He's nine. He shouldn't have to decide whether soccer is worth the pain.

Neither should yours.

EDIT: A few parents have messaged asking if this is okay to use alongside what their doctor already told them to do.

Yes. It's not a replacement for rest, ice, or your doctor's plan. Nothing here asks you to skip that.

It's support during the hours he's actually loading his knee, which is the part rest never covers.

If you want to ask your doctor first, ask. Mine had no problem with it. He was the one who suggested support in the first place.

Same link: https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

P.S. I keep coming back to that soccer bag.

$400 of custom support. Made for his feet. Sitting under a sandwich.

Not because they didn't work. They did.

Because he was nine and they hurt and I couldn't win that fight every single morning.

Support only counts when it's under the foot. That's the whole thing I got wrong for a year.

Four pairs. His cleats, his sneakers, his school shoes, and a spare: https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

P.P.S. He limped for almost a full year.

I sat in the car after every practice and told myself the same thing I'd been told.

He'll grow out of it.

I wrote the email. I had my finger on the button.

And the whole time, the answer was in the shoes I picked up off the floor every night.

I got there late. But he's still playing.

Your kid is still lacing up.

Still throwing the bag in the back seat.

Still asking what's for dinner.

You have not run out of time.

Watch his feet before you let him quit: https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

=====

Why Footstr works when the other stuff didn't.

Most parents end up stuck between two bad options.

Option one is the pharmacy insert. Soft, cheap, completely flat. It just follows the foot down as the arch collapses. Putting one inside your kid's shoe is basically the same as not having one.

Option two is the custom orthotic. Rigid, expensive, bulky inside a cleat. When kids actually wear them, the support is real. But most kids don't wear them.

$300 to $800 for a device that ends up in the bottom of a soccer bag. And growing kids may need replacements every six to eighteen months.

Footstr sits in between.

1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT

There's real structure underneath the arch, not a flat piece of foam. But the insole flexes as the child walks, runs, cuts, and plays instead of locking the foot in place.

It helps reduce that excessive inward rolling while the child is wearing it, without the rigid feel that makes kids pull them out.

2 - HEEL CUSHIONING

Running, jumping, and landing put repeated impact on growing feet. Footstr cushions the heel so there's a softer place to land during the activities that usually lead to complaints.

3 - THE STRENGTHENING PROGRAM

This is the part most parents don't expect.

The insole and the exercises have two different jobs.

The insole supports the arch and heel during activity. The exercises give the muscles around the feet and arches something to work on outside the shoe.

Support during activity. Strengthening work over time.

That's what makes this feel like a plan instead of another thing you buy after your kid is already hurting.

=====

What parents usually notice.

WEEKS 1 - 2

The first thing you'll probably notice isn't that the pain disappears overnight.

It's that your kid keeps wearing them.

No arguments. No bargaining. No finding them at the bottom of a sports bag.

They stay in the shoe because they're comfortable enough to stay in the shoe.

That alone is a win if you've been through custom orthotics.

WEEKS 3 - 4

This is when most parents start seeing the pattern change.

The car ride home from practice sounds different. Your kid is talking about the game instead of their feet.

The ice pack hasn't moved from the freezer.

The old cycle of practice, pain, ice, rest doesn't start automatically after every hard session.

WEEK 6+

The sore days stop running your week.

Your kid is more active because they're not managing pain all the time. They're finishing practices, playing full games, coming home tired for normal kid reasons.

They might not even mention their feet anymore.

=====

Common questions.

"Will my kid actually wear these?"

This is the most common question we get, and it's the right one.

Footstr is softer underneath the foot than custom orthotics, but still has structure underneath the arch. Most kids forget they're wearing them after the first day. If your child pulled custom orthotics out of their shoes because they were too hard and bulky, that's exactly why Footstr was designed differently.

"How is this different from the pharmacy insoles I already tried?"

Pharmacy insoles are flat. They follow the foot down as the arch collapses. Footstr has structured arch support and heel cushioning. There's a real difference between something soft and something that actually supports the foot during activity.

"Will they fit inside cleats?"

Yes. They're designed for the shoes kids actually wear, including soccer cleats, basketball shoes, and sneakers.

"My kid's doctor said they'll grow out of it."

Maybe they will. But a study of 92,000 adolescents found that kids with moderate to severe flat feet had nearly double the rate of knee pain and low back pain compared to kids with normal arches. Another study from 2025 found that flat-footed kids scored 42 percent higher on a clinical pain scale and were measurably less active than their classmates.

Your child might grow out of it. They also might not. And right now, while they're growing, their feet are underneath them for every practice, every game, and every school day.

Giving them support during that time is a pretty reasonable place to start.

=====

"Watching my kids walk off the field without limping felt like a small parenting victory."

=====

Why waiting can cost more than you think.

Flat feet and overpronation don't always stay the same. The complaints can get worse.

"A little sore after practice" becomes limping to the car.

"He's just tired" becomes asking to sit out.

"He'll grow out of it" becomes watching him lose interest in the sport he used to beg to play.

One season he's talking about the game on the way home. The next season he stops asking if today is a soccer day.

Kids don't always tell you their feet hurt. Sometimes they just get quieter.

=====

"He says they feel like walking on pillows. He doesn't even know they're in there anymore."

=====

One more thing before you decide.

Your child doesn't just wear one pair of shoes.

They go from school shoes to sneakers to cleats. If Footstr is only in one pair, they have support part of the day and nothing the rest of it.

That's why the 4-pack exists.

Four pairs. One for school shoes. One for sneakers. One for cleats. One for another pair they wear regularly.

No moving one insole around. No choosing which activity gets the support and which one doesn't.
